The collar's inner band had sunk between swollen scales. When he laid two fingers near it, heat struck his knuckles in three uneven pulses. Dovra's lungs answered with a dry scrape. A seed of glass swelled at the corner of their mouth. They spat it onto the tile before it could close over a tooth.

"How far did you walk yesterday?" Ordran asked.

"To the window."

"Six paces," Neris said. "Without help."

"Back?"

Dovra's eye stayed on him. "No."

Neris caught up the wet sheet. "They had transferred an attack that morning. You cannot measure recovery on the same day."

"Which day would please you?"

"Three quiet mornings. That was the condition. We nearly had two before this week."

"Last month it was one," Dovra said.

"Last month you could still unfold your wing."

"Which is why the condition moved."

Ordran pressed at the base of the clear scale and felt no give. The hardening had reached deeper than the color showed. "A full draw now will seal the joints under the breast. You may get a few breaths afterward. Not enough to leave."

Neris's fingers tightened in the sheet. "Then take the surplus out of Dovra. You did it the first night."

"Dovra took it out of you. I kept their airway open."

"You built the focus."

"And someone rebuilt the lock."

Dovra's foreclaw slid across the tile and covered the iron box. "Ivara did."

The queen was filling basins from a copper cistern. Water rang against metal; she let it run long after the first basin overflowed.

Neris looked at her. "You said he required the seal."

Ivara shut the tap. "You were burning again. The catch had opened. Dovra had not yet left. We needed time to prepare another room."

"You told me the dragon physician had revised his work."

"I ordered the armorer to revise it."

There it was, smaller than a confession and harder. Water crawled over the tabletop and dropped onto the floor.

Neris pulled the ring of keys from her belt. "And you gave this to me."

"The following week."

"After Dovra asked you twice."

Dovra lifted their head. The movement made the glassed wing fingers chatter. "I asked at sunrise. I had offered until sunrise."

Neris flinched as though the room had snapped a spark at her. "You stayed."

"The door was closed."

"You could have broken it."

Dovra's claw left the lock and settled near Neris's bare foot, careful not to touch. "With you behind it."

The princess took one step back. The house keys knocked together in her hand.

Ordran reached toward the lock with a probe. Dovra caught the leather cuff of his sleeve between two talons. Weak as they were, they stopped his hand without effort.

"If I quiet the vanes," he said, "I can split the armorer's rivets before the next rise."

"And her fire?" Dovra asked.

"Her mother gets her to the baths. I treat her there."

"Before she knows?"

"Before she stops us."

Dovra released his sleeve. "Put the probe away."

He did not. "You want the collar off or you do not."

"I want your hand away from my throat."

Ordran heard his own certainty a moment too late. He put the probe back in its slot.

Neris laughed once, without amusement. "Your rescue seems to be going badly. Mother, take him home. When the north room is lined, we can discuss a controlled release."

"The north room will take a month," Ivara said.

"Then the lower cistern. Two weeks."

"There is no two weeks," Ordran said.

"Three days. I can fast. I can sleep packed in ice. Dovra will not need to draw."

A glass bulb rolled from beneath the dragon's folded wing. It wandered through the spilled water, trailing steam. Dovra tried to move clear of it and their foreleg folded. The breast struck tile with a crystalline note.

Neris dropped beside them. "Easy. Don't push."

"Open the collar," Ordran said.

"Not while they cannot stand."

"They cannot stand because you keep the collar closed."

"I kept everyone alive."

"You kept changing the morning."

Heat flashed through the wet floor under Ordran's knees.

Neris froze. The sheet on her shoulder began to dry from the center outward. Beneath the skin of her neck, a thin orange line climbed toward her jaw.

The collar clicked twice.

Dovra's head came up. "No."

The vanes all turned toward Neris.

Ordran tore the soft-copper roll from his case. The harness was only arranged metal until living heat entered it; now the original path opened between Neris and Dovra, and the royal lock held that path against the dragon's body. No intention lived in the silver. It pulled because it had been made to pull and prevented from letting go.

The first forced draw hit.

Neris's rising line vanished. Dovra arched so hard that their horns scored plaster. White light spread under the transparent breast scales. Their cough threw three hot glass bulbs across the room. One burst against a basin. Another spun toward Ordran, and he trapped it beneath his case with the sole of his boot.

He drove a flattened loop of copper into the teeth of the iron box.

The box snapped down on it.

The draw broke unevenly. Half the light drained from Dovra's chest; half the orange line blazed back along Neris's arms. She screamed and clawed the wet sheet away before it could steam against her skin.

Ivara seized the key ring.

Neris struck her hand aside. "Mine."

"Then use it."

"Not in here. Not with the curtains—"

The casement drapes had begun to smoke.

"Baths," Ordran said. "The west shutters. Now."

He kept one hand on the copper loop. The royal box ground it down with short clicks. When the soft metal sheared, the whole draw would reopen.

Ivara ripped a drape from its hooks and stamped the smoking hem in the spilled water. She flung open the tiled doors behind Dovra. Cold damp came through, along with the smell of old stone.

Neris tried to stand and went down on one palm. Fire curled between her fingers without consuming them. "Dovra, take only enough for me to walk."

The dragon gathered their feet under them. "No."

"You won't reach the shutters if I cannot move."

Dovra lurched forward. "Then crawl."

Ivara crouched, took her adult daughter beneath the arms, and dragged her onto the wet tile. Neris cursed and fought for footing, but when her heels found the shallow drain she pushed with them.

The old bath was one long chamber built against the outer wall, its empty pools sunk below a gallery of blue tile. At the far end, tall steam shutters opened onto a sloping lead roof above the marsh side of the palace. The wheel that lifted them hung high, its chain orange with rust. One of the fresh glass bulbs rolled ahead through the rainwater and came to rest six paces from the first pool step. Dovra halted as if counting how many of those paces their legs could bear.

Ordran walked beside the collar, holding the copper jam in place. Dovra's right forefoot skidded on the bulb. It cracked flat beneath their palm, leaving a thin red line across one pad. They did not stop. Neris came behind, leaning backward into Ivara's body as heat pushed from her in waves.

"Cloths in the drain," Ordran called. "Neck, armpits, inner thighs. Don't wrap her."

"We know how to cool a fever," Ivara said.

"This is not a fever."

The queen bit off her next answer. She laid Neris on the lowest broad step, soaked two cloths, and pressed them where Ordran had said. When Neris twisted away, Ivara followed rather than pinning her flat. The crown finally came loose and rang into the empty pool. Neither woman looked at it.

Ordran braced Dovra near the outer wall and reached for his wedge.

"Forefeet here," he said. "When I split the hinge, lift against—"

Dovra put one bleeding talon on the wedge and pressed it to the tile.

"If I tell you to stop after you begin," they asked, "will your hand stop?"

The copper in the lock gave another crushed click.

Ordran looked at the tool beneath Dovra's claw. Cutting now would be fast. The stored fire might recoil through the open path into both bodies; it might also free the dragon before anyone could change their mind.

He opened his fingers and left the wedge on the floor.

"The jam may hold for two minutes," he said. "If Neris turns the key before it fails, the vanes will flatten and I can cut the cold hinge. If I split it while the path is open, the recoil may stop either heart. If the jam breaks and you take the whole rise, the glass will reach your chest before we can get you out."

Dovra moved their talon off the wedge.

"What do you want?" Ordran asked.

"No more of her fire. Collar off. Shutters open."

"All right."

Neris made a broken sound from the pool step. "Dovra. Look at me."

The dragon did.

"Until he gets the shutters up," she said. "A sip. Not the crest. You know how fast I burn when the air turns cold."

"No."

"I will open it after."

Dovra's answer was a rasp of breath. "No."

Neris shook her head, trying to move the future by force of habit. "When the cloths are cold, then. When Mother has me in the pool."

The copper loop shrieked inside the lock.

Neris grabbed the key ring. Her fingers were too slick to separate the iron key from the smaller brass ones. "Mother, order—"

"The long key," Ivara said, pushing a soaked cloth under Neris's wrist. "Turn it left."

"Order them!"

Ivara set her knees against Neris's hips as another spasm bowed her off the step. "I did."

That was all she managed before Neris's heat threw steam into both their faces.

The jam split.

Dovra's scales flashed.

Neris found the long key. She dragged herself across two wet tiles and thrust it into the royal box. The metal burned her palm; she lost it, caught it against the collar, and tried again. Ordran held the harness steady without touching her hand.

"Left," Ivara said.

Neris turned.

The box opened with a blunt clack. Every copper vane fell away from Dovra's throat. Fire surged back through Neris so quickly that she collapsed against the dragon's shoulder, then recoiled before Dovra could be made to hold her weight.

Ivara caught her.

Ordran slid the cold wedge under the altered hinge. "Dovra?"

"Cut."

He struck once. The armorer's rivet broke. Silver sprang wide, tearing one glass-thin scale but carrying no heat with it. Dovra shook the collar onto the tiles.

The dragon did not wait.

They limped to the steam shutters while Ordran climbed the wheel housing. The chain would not move. Ivara had laid her daughter back in the rain channel and was holding soaked cloths at her neck with one hand, bracing her shoulders with the other.

Neris reached toward Dovra. Whether for help or to stop them, Ordran could not tell. Her arm fell short. Flame sheeted across the rainwater and vanished in a blast of white vapor.

Dovra rose onto their hind legs and hooked both foreclaws through the lowest shutter slat. The glassed right wing stayed clamped to their side. Ordran knocked the corroded axle pin loose with the heel of his cutter. Dovra hauled; the wheel spun hard enough to wrench Ordran's shoulder, and the shutters climbed.

Cold night opened above the roof.

Dovra shoved their head and shoulders through. The broken scale at their neck wept one dark line. They paused only to pull the injured forefoot onto the sill.

Behind them, Neris began to burn in earnest.

Ordran left the wheel propped with his case and went to her. Ivara had gotten both arms around Neris's ribs, keeping her upright so the heat could escape without the princess striking her head on stone. The queen's wet sleeves steamed. Blisters rose on the hand that supported Neris's jaw.

"Keep her facing the vent," Ordran said. "Don't let her breathe the steam."

The shutters banged once in the wind.

Dovra squeezed onto the lead roof. For a moment their clear wing fingers snagged between two slats. They folded tighter, worked free, and slid out of sight.

Ordran heard claws cross the roof. Then a heavy scramble, a scrape of glass on lead, and silence.

He could not turn. Neris's pulse was running too fast beneath his fingers. Fire moved under her skin in branching seams. He changed the cloth at her throat, then another, while Ivara held her through each convulsion and took the curses that came whenever Neris found breath.

The first wingbeat sounded below the window.

The second struck harder. On the third, a pale body rose past the open shutters. Dovra's right wing opened late and crooked, but it opened. They cleared the palace wall and dropped toward the black marsh, where cold mist lay between the reeds.

Neris saw them. Her mouth formed the dragon's name, but the oncoming crest crushed it into a gasp.

Ordran could have shouted. Dovra had turned at smaller sounds during that first night. They might have turned now from care, from fear, from the old practiced reach of Neris's fire.

He put both hands to the work in front of him and did not call.

The crest lasted long enough for the rain channel to run hot. Neris's hair smoldered at the ends. A patch of skin along her left arm blistered, and her breath caught twice until Ordran levered her jaw forward. Ivara stayed on her knees behind her, thighs locked around her daughter's hips, one burned hand supporting her chest. She asked for cloth, then water, then another cloth.

At last the orange seams beneath Neris's skin shortened. The flame at her hands guttered. She sagged into Ivara so abruptly that the queen nearly struck the pool edge with her shoulder.

"Still here," Ordran said when Neris's eyes opened.

She coughed. "That is not a prognosis."

"No."

"Tomorrow?"

"If you are breathing tomorrow, I will know more."

She swallowed, each breath a shallow effort. "Come anyway."

Ordran checked her pupils and said nothing he could not guarantee. Her pulse was slowing. The burns were survivable. The next rise might be gentler or worse; there was no collar now to hide it from her until it had already begun.

Ivara shifted one numb leg and tightened her hold before Neris could slide. Her crown lay at the bottom of the empty pool, bright under a skin of rainwater. The opened key remained in the iron box across the room. No one reached for either.

Beyond the shutters, morning grayed the marsh. Dovra was already a narrow, uneven shadow over it, flying west without circling. Ordran watched for one breath, then knelt to replace the cooling cloth in Ivara's burned hand.

stories.title: Coiled Together
stories.prompt: Everyone knows the serpentfolk lure travelers into their caves and devour them. When you wake wrapped tightly in the coils of one of their most feared queens, however, she seems less interested in eating you than in keeping you—and insists that you were the one who begged her not to let go.
stories.body:
# Coiled Together

My first clear thought was that I could not measure the room.

A scout measures before he decides anything: six strides to the door, a handspan of loose scree under the left boot, enough headroom to swing a blade. I had no stride, no ground to test, and barely enough breath to count. A scaled body thicker than a rain barrel crossed my shins. Another turn covered my hips. A third held my left arm against my ribs and ran behind my shoulders, warm and hard as sunlit masonry.

I drew one careful breath. The turn across my chest rose with it and settled when I exhaled.

I tried the right hand first. Free. Both feet answered when I flexed them, though they could go nowhere. My shirt and trousers were wet but fastened. Belt buckled. Boots laced. No blood on my fingertips when I felt my face, no pain from ribs or spine, only a fever pounding behind my eyes.

Then the thing holding me lifted its head.

The woman above the coils had black hair braided with flat gold rings and a face the road sketches had made cruder than it was. Green slit-pupiled eyes followed my hand to my throat. Below a sleeveless gray wrap, bronze skin gave way to dark-gold scales. The rest of her filled the low chamber in overlapping curves.

I was thirty-four years old and had spent fourteen of them finding routes around hazards. None of that training suggested a useful direction.

“Sivareth,” I said.

Her mouth opened just enough to show two fine points. “You remember my name. That is something.”

Humans called her the Gilded Hunger. The same accounts that named her said travelers entered the Hushvault and did not come out. I had never considered whether an adult serpentfolk queen might look tired.

“Move this turn down,” I said, touching the scales over my left forearm. “Two finger-widths. I want my wrist.”

She moved it at once. Not a twitch or a grudging slackening: the whole heavy length rolled below my elbow and left my hand free.

I pulled the arm to my chest and worked each finger. “Now loosen the one over my ribs.”

It opened enough for me to fill my lungs. No farther.

“You make small requests very clearly,” she said.

“Small mistakes kill scouts.” I pushed at the coil over my hips. It did not shift. “Take all of them off.”

“No.”

A request could move a coil. It could not yet get me out of them.

“You are unhurt,” she continued. “You are also fevered, confused, and surrounded by your own hunters. When those conditions change, I will reconsider.”

“My own people are a caravan. My knife and pack?”

“Dry. Behind me.”

“Put them where I can see them.”

She watched my face, then reached into the curve of her body and set both on a shelf cut into the wall. The pack was closed. My knife remained in its sheath.

Another burst of glass-rain rasped across the mountain outside, sharper than sleet and too heavy for sand. Water drummed somewhere beneath us. The chamber held three hooded lamps, a stack of fur blankets, and a black opening in the floor whose far wall I could not see. We were deep enough that the storm sounded like a saw working through bone.

“How did I get here?”

“You came through the eastern mouth carrying a scent meant for me. The shelf beneath you had been cut. It broke. I caught you above the lower shaft.” Her eyes narrowed. “You told me not to let go.”

The last thing I remembered cleanly was Captain Halvek Prynn pressing a copper charm into my palm below the ridge. A ward, he had called it. The memory after that came apart: rain on my eyelids, a yellow spark in wet rock, somebody ordering me farther in.

“I don't remember asking you.”

“You did not ask. You shouted until your voice failed, then begged.”

“That was over a hole.”

“It was.”

“This is a bed of furs.”

Sivareth glanced down as though checking the distinction. “The hole was less comfortable.”

Her humor had no softness in it. She knew exactly how much of the room she occupied, exactly how quickly she could close the breath she had returned.

I found the cut ends of a leather cord at my neck. “The charm.”

She reached for a shallow stone bowl near the lamps. Inside lay a thumb-long cage of twisted copper, split open along one edge and bundled in waxed cloth. A dirty amber pellet glistened through the gap.

“Do not warm it again,” she said. “It speaks in heat and musk. It led me from the clutch stair to your fall.”

“You expect me to believe a human lure caught a queen?”

“Caught?” The membranes at her temples lifted. “It offended my nose in my own halls. I went to remove it.”

She tipped the bowl close enough for me to inspect without touching. The copper had been twisted square instead of round, the way Prynn's supply cages were made so they would not roll off a wagon bed. One side bore three file strokes. I had cut those marks myself when I inventoried his stores two nights before.

Heat from the lamp softened the pellet despite the waxed cloth. A sweet animal smell climbed from it, followed by the taste of old pennies at the back of my tongue.

My memory gave me a wet thumb rubbing that same resin over the charm. Prynn's left hand, the smallest finger ending at the first joint. His other hand tightened the cord around my neck.

*It'll turn them away, Kerric. You take the inside line.*

The chamber tilted. I shut my eyes until the pounding eased.

“It raises your heat,” Sivareth said. “It tangles the nearest memories. That is what this piece did to you. I will not pretend to know every mixture humans have cooked.”

“How do you know what this one does?”

“A man wore one here last spring. He chose the clutch stair after I warned him away.” One pointed tooth touched her lower lip. “He improved my education. He did not improve the stories told about me.”

I looked toward the dark opening in the floor. “Did you eat him?”

“No.”

“Did you kill him?”

“Yes.”

She offered no excuse, and I did not ask for one. A nest under threat could make a wolf dangerous without making every warning about wolves false. The old road tales had kept me from other caves. They might yet keep me alive in this one.

Sivareth shifted a lower coil. My fevered muscles yielded to the warmth before I could stop them. Relief traveled up my legs, bodily and immediate. It changed nothing about who had decided I could not stand.

Her eyes noticed the easing in me.

“My muscles are reacting to heat,” I said. “Don't call it an answer.”

“I did not ask a question.” Yet the turn over my thighs settled more closely.

I tapped it with two fingers. “Back where it was.”

She moved it back.

Across the chamber, a pale sheet of mineral had been fitted into the rock like a cloudy window. Gold veins wandered through it. Sivareth extinguished the nearest lamp, and warmth appeared on the sheet in blurred islands: one great amber mass around a smaller red center, then six dim upright smears beyond us, arranged in two levels along the rising passage.

“Six bodies,” I said.

“Six fires in human shapes.”

“Can that show weapons?”

“It shows heat and position. A hand leaving a chest. A head turning. Nothing of iron, words, or purpose.” She placed one claw beneath the highest three smears. “These have waited above the narrow throat since before you woke.”

“Could be my caravan looking for me.”

“Then your caravan searches with remarkable patience.”

One shape leaned toward another. The mineral recorded only their changing heat, not what passed between them. Useful evidence, incomplete by design. I trusted it more for that.

Water struck below with a deeper boom. A cold thread crept across the chamber floor from the eastern passage and vanished into the shaft.

Sivareth looked at it. “The upper drains are blocked. If the rain holds, the lower chambers flood. I will move you farther inside.”

“How far?”

“Beyond the clutch stair.”

The loops around me tightened by the breadth of a fingernail, an unconscious answer before her words.

“You would carry me deeper while armed people wait at the mouth.”

“I would keep what I saved out of their hands.”

“What you saved is listening.”

Her chin lifted. “And would walk directly under them if released.”

“Probably. I need to see the route before I believe your reading of it.”

“Your fever makes the floor move.”

“Then the floor will tell me how sick I am.” I pointed to the shelf. “Put the pack at my feet. Put the knife on it. Remove every coil.”

“I said no.”

“The fall ended. So did that order. If you want a prisoner, say prisoner.”

The largest bend of her body rose behind her. Scales whispered over stone. For one hard moment I understood how a hunter might die before he saw the strike.

“You entered my home scented for my death,” she said. “Your companions choke my drains. My clutch is below them. I am entitled to very little patience.”

“I did not cut your drains, and I did not know what I carried. You cannot stack me with the things you are protecting.”

Her gaze stayed on the loop across my knees. It took no heat-reading stone to see she wanted it left there.

Then she drew back.

The turn at my chest went first. The weight over my hips slid away, followed by the loops at my knees and boots. Cold found every wet seam in my clothing. I pushed upright on the furs and waited for the cave to stop rocking. Sivareth did not touch me.

She set the pack at my feet and laid the sheathed knife across it, hilt toward my right hand. The wax-wrapped lure remained in the stone bowl.

“That too,” I said.

“It sickens you.”

“It is evidence against Prynn. Fold the cloth over it and wrap it again.”

She folded a second square of waxed cloth around the charm, tied the bundle, and placed it in the outer pocket of my pack. Then she withdrew far enough that open floor lay between us and the eastern passage.

“Nothing of mine touches you now, Kerric Alver.” Her voice had gone formal and flat. “I dislike it.”

“You don't have to like a route for it to be open.”

I strapped on the knife, shouldered the pack, and stood. My knees held. Fever pulled the lamps into short golden streaks, but I could walk a straight chalk line between two cracks in the floor.

When the last warmth of her coils left my palms, memory returned in a flash no longer than a blink: the shelf dropping; my body swinging over black water; Sivareth braced sideways in a fissure, one arm locked around my wrist. My grip had slipped on her wet scales. A gold length had whipped up from below and closed around my waist.

*Don't let go. Please. Don't let go.*

Her answer had come through bared teeth: *Then stop fighting my hold.*

I opened my eyes in the chamber. Sivareth had not moved to reclaim me.

“I remember the shaft,” I said.

Something in her expression sharpened with hope.

“I meant it there,” I added.

The hope narrowed, but did not vanish. “You were less exact while falling.”

“I am going to the eastern mouth.”

“I will not follow unless you call.”

I left her beside the heat-sheet.

The eastern passage climbed forty paces from her chamber to a gray blade of stormlight. Ten paces in, three white quartz ribs crossed the floor. Beyond them the roof lowered and the ground split: the main runoff gnawed westward through a central trench, while a dry shelf hugged the south wall above it. That shelf ran toward the entrance, then broadened into a gallery overlooking the narrowest part of the tunnel.

I crouched behind the third rib and read the damage. Someone had driven two iron anchors into opposite walls above the throat. Dark rope vanished over the gallery lip. Net rig. On the south side, an old cross-drain should have carried water from a swollen wall basin across the gallery and down a sink on the north. The hunters had rammed a canvas bundle into its mouth and lashed it to a piton, keeping their perch dry. Water trembled behind the plug and spilled around its edges into the lower runnel—the cold thread already reaching Sivareth's chamber.

The plug was a foolish convenience. Cut its lashing and the backed water would scour across the gallery before dropping into the north sink. The outer neck of the shelf was shale. One hard rush might split it and leave anyone on the inner gallery stranded above the trench.

The lashing hung an arm's reach above the tunnel floor. Easy to cut if no one shot me first.

I crawled beneath the gallery until voices resolved through the water noise.

“Net pair, wait for the shoulders,” Prynn said. He was close, just above and east of me. “Bow line takes the high turns. Nobody looses while Kerric is on top.”

A woman answered, “And if he's underneath?”

“Then aim better. The lure got her here. We don't waste the opening.”

“The shelf dropped with him on it.”

“I know where I put the wedge.” Prynn's impatience was familiar enough to raise a dozen camp mornings around me. “Watch the chalk mark. Gold crosses, you pull.”

Prynn's sequence told me enough. He had weakened the shelf. He expected Sivareth to bring his bait back. Whether I could crawl away afterward belonged to nobody's assignment.

One boot scraped on the gallery above me. I backed out on hands and knees, rose behind the quartz ribs, and walked to the chamber under my own power.

Sivareth had gathered herself beside the heat-sheet. Six shapes still burned across it. She read my face before I spoke.

“Which claim did the stone fail to prove?” she asked.

“All of them. Prynn proved the rest.” I dropped the pack but kept the knife. “Two on the net, three bows, Prynn calling the drop. He cut the shelf himself.”

Her upper body lowered. “Then I will clear my threshold.”

“Rush the gallery and they drop barbs across your spine. Wait here and the blocked cross-drain sends half the storm toward your clutch.”

“I can endure barbs.”

“Can the chambers below endure the water?”

The end of her tail struck stone once. “Speak, route scout.”

I scratched the passage in the grit: chamber, quartz ribs, central trench, gallery, cross-drain, mouth. “Their dry ledge is the trap and the weakness. The plug is here. I can cut it from below. The wash takes their footing and their anchors, then drops north instead of running toward your clutch.”

“You cannot stand beneath five hunters long enough to cut anything.”

“No.” I looked at the broad shield of her outer coils. “Carry me to it.”

She went motionless.

“You required distance,” she said.

“I required release. I got it.” I stepped close enough to point along her body without touching. “Now I'm asking for cover. Keep my right arm clear. Hold me firmly enough to cross the trench, loosely enough that I can turn to the lashing. Bring me back past the three white ribs and set me down there.”

“If an arrow finds a gap?”

“Close the gap. Not my lungs.”

“And if you order me open before the ribs?”

“You open. I take whatever the trench does.”

Sivareth looked at the knife in my right hand. “You would keep that where it can cut the canvas.”

“Yes.”

“And me.”

“Yes.”

Her teeth showed. “I will watch that hand.”

“If I miss the rope, move me two fingers higher.”

Her lower coils parted, leaving a space before her. “Then tell me where to put you.”

The old road warnings came readily: never enter a serpent den; never accept a queen's gift; never let scales close behind you. None of them had been written for a drain lashing beneath five bows.

“Sivareth, hold me and carry me to the cross-drain. Bring me back to the ribs on those terms.”

She came forward slowly. One coil curved under my boots and raised me above the wet floor. A second supported my hips. The highest loop passed over my left shoulder and across my chest, leaving my knife arm outside. She adjusted once when I could not fill a breath, then waited.

I twisted toward an imaginary overhead knot. My shoulder moved. My wrist reached. Both boots stayed braced.

“Go,” I said.

Sivareth drove east, her scales finding wet stone in a fast alternating rhythm.

Her scales found purchase on both sides of the trench. At the quartz ribs she raised the outer turn over my head. The gallery filled the low ceiling ahead; I could see the net's lower edge folded against its lip and three bow tips between stone teeth.

Prynn shouted, “Mark!”

The net fell before Sivareth reached the chalk line.

She reared into it rather than away. Barbs rang across her upper coils and hooked between two plates. The turn around my chest locked hard enough to halt me, not crush me. An arrow struck the curve above my shoulder and skidded into the trench.

“Lashing,” she hissed.

I leaned from her shelter. The canvas plug bulged over my head, its cord vibrating against the piton. My first cut glanced off wet rope. Fever doubled the knot. I hooked my left hand through the cord, pulled it low, and sawed twice.

A hunter swung from the gallery lip onto the narrow south shelf beside us, reaching for my wrist. Sivareth's free hand caught his bow and broke it against the wall. She could have taken the arm with it. Her claws stopped a finger from his sleeve.

The cord parted.

The plug came out like a kicked door. Black water burst sideways across the gallery, carrying glass grit, shale chips, and the hunters' canvas. The man on the shelf threw himself onto the lip. One net anchor tore free; the other wrenched the barbs across Sivareth's scales before the whole rig sagged into the trench.

She turned around me, took the pull on her outermost coil, and drove west. Behind us, the cross-drain ate through the shale neck in three loud cracks. A section of the hunters' path dropped away. All six crowded onto the surviving inner gallery, separated from the mouth by a widening rush of water and from us by the central trench.

They were stranded, not defeated. Two still had bows. Another had a climbing coil looped over one shoulder. Given time after the storm, they would rig a way out.

“Kerric!” Prynn gripped an iron anchor above the broken shelf. “Throw the knife. We can set a traverse.”

I kept the blade against my forearm as Sivareth backed toward the quartz. “There's a sound crack above your left shoulder and a spare piton under the net rope. Use those.”

“You're leaving with that thing?”

The coil shielding me rose. Sivareth turned her head, and every hunter on the gallery went still.

“If any of you descend toward my clutch,” she said, “I will not strand you twice.”

Prynn's mouth tightened. “I brought you into the company, Kerric.”

“You put a wedge under my route.”

“One scale clears every winter debt we carry.”

I pointed west. Sivareth moved.

Water poured cleanly into the north sink now. The lower runnel was already shrinking. Sivareth crossed the first white quartz rib, then the second. Her forward coil passed the third before she lowered my boots to dry stone beyond it.

“Open,” I said.

Every turn left me.

No last squeeze, no delay while she measured the arrows behind us. Her body slid away before I had finished planting my heels. I stood alone on the chamber side of the ribs, knife in hand, with the western cleft open behind me.

Sivareth remained between me and the hunters. Two barbs hung from a scored outer scale. She pulled them free and dropped them into the water.

“The western cleft climbs to open ground,” she said without looking at me. “The rain should soften before midday. I will point out the beginning. I will not accompany you.”

“And Prynn?”

“He has the crack you gave him. If he comes lower, he has my warning.”

I sheathed the knife and returned to the chamber for my pack. The waxed bundle containing the lure still sat in its outer pocket. I could take it down to the caravan, along with Prynn's own inventory marks and whatever account I chose to give. None of that required another hour inside the Hushvault.

My knees shook when I bent to lift the pack. Fever tilted the floor. When the waxed lure knocked against the pocket, I gripped the strap until my knuckles hurt. On the far shelf sat smoked river fish, flatbread, and a pot that smelled of pepperleaf broth.

“I will eat before I take the western route,” I said. “One bowl. I leave when the rain eases.”

Sivareth looked back.

“You have made a remarkably small visit of being devoured.”

“I haven't tasted the broth.”

She considered that with royal seriousness, then drew the pot toward the lamps. I sat on a separate folded fur with my pack beside my left hand and the passage in sight. Cold water had filled both boots during the crossing. My toes were beginning to ache.

Sivareth's tail lay three feet away. She did not move it closer.

“One turn around the boots,” I said. “Below the ankles. Leave room for me to pull free.”

“How much pressure?”

“Enough to warm the leather.”

The end of her coil circled my boots and stopped short of closing. I tested one heel; it lifted easily. Sivareth set a bowl of broth in my hands.

“My first question,” I said, “is about the hunter who reached your clutch stair.”

Her eyes narrowed over the steam. “Then eat before I answer.”

stories.title: Held Together
stories.prompt: a Married hero couple going through a rough patch get captured by a married villain couple and are surprised at how healthy their relationship is.
stories.body:
# Held Together

When Aveline Ormont woke, her husband was counting under his breath.

“Eight, nine, ten—”

“Don’t move.”

Harlan Ives stopped at eleven. His back was pressed to hers, close enough that she could feel him breathe and not close enough to tell whether the shallow breaths meant pain. Four steel bands fixed their wrists and ankles to a low frame. A fifth crossed Aveline’s chest. The room around them was windowless, faced in gray ceramic, with a narrow vent cut high in the wall.

Their masks were still on. After nine years of marriage, Tensile and Sideslip were names they used for reports, witnesses, and the occasional child who wanted an autograph. In private, Aveline called him Harlan. For most of the last six weeks, she had used his name only when patrol required it.

“I wasn’t moving,” he said. “I was inventorying.”

“Out loud?”

“I hoped numbers might lure you back to consciousness. You respect them more than I do.”

Beyond the wall, the stolen phase-key gave off a glassy, rising hum. The sound put the loading dock back into Aveline’s head: the key suspended in its transport cage; Sana Dacre’s gloved hand reaching through a sealed panel by way of her husband’s folded space; Harlan shouting the old three-count. Aveline’s tensile field had released the dock cable when she told it to. The force had struck four heartbeats later, after Harlan had committed to his phase. The concrete bucked. Keaton Dacre folded the distance between two pillars, and the heroes ran straight into a waiting net.

“You went before three,” Aveline said.

“There it is.”

“Did you?”

“You pulled before two.”

“I released on two. The floor moved late.”

He was quiet for half a breath. “That is a fascinating choice of verb tense.”

Aveline hooked a thread of force between her right wrist and the frame. Her field caught the band’s tension as if it were a wire she could pluck, stretch, and cast into another anchor.

The wall clicked.

The frame twisted beneath them. Harlan’s shoulder vanished from her back for an instant; his attempt to phase out took weight off one side. A black node in the wall spun, converting both changes into torque. The bands cinched at once. Five seconds later the force Aveline had dismissed returned through the frame in a dull kick that drove the chest strap against her ribs.

Harlan sucked air through his teeth. “For the next minute, can we postpone the demonstration portion of your prosecution?”

She made herself let the field go slack. The room was a balance trap. Any sudden change in load—pull, impact, mass disappearing into phase—turned the restraint spindle forward. The delayed kick had turned it twice.

“Damping lattice,” she said. “Four wall nodes, perhaps six. Shared spindle. It winds on an unbalanced load.”

“So if neither of us does anything stupid, we die of old age in a tasteful ceramic box.”

“The Dacres don’t kill captives.”

“Comforting distinction from the people who put us in a box.”

Metal rolled in the room above them. A drawer opened, then another.

“Narrow jaw,” Sana Dacre said through the vent.

“Retired,” Keaton answered.

“You retired my extractor jaw during an extraction?”

“It has a crack.”

“It has a scratch.”

“It sings when you load it.”

“Everything sings when you load it. That’s what load is.”

Keaton’s footsteps crossed the ceiling. The second drawer shut. “Broad jaw, top tray. Two braces.”

“Seven extra minutes.”

“Six if you eat while I fit it.”

Paper rustled. Something slid over a workbench.

“Mustard?” Sana asked.

“Your half is innocent.”

“You remembered.”

“I remember plenty of things that don’t shoot wire at me.”

The Dacres had been married eleven years and stealing together for almost as long. Latchkey and Parallax in the case files: a woman who fixed openings and cable-lines to surfaces with black metal latches, and a man who bent the distance between those anchors. They had stolen the key, captured two intervening heroes, and remembered how one another took a sandwich.

Harlan tipped his head until his hair brushed hers. “I find this deeply offensive.”

“The mustard?”

“We got kidnapped by adults.”

“Listen for the guard rotation.”

“Yes, counsel.”

Keaton wound a kitchen timer. Its ticking came through the vent beneath the key’s hum.

On the ceramic opposite Aveline, a pale hand appeared with no arm attached. Its fingers measured the distance between two wall nodes, repeated the motion, then rested against an empty seam. One of Keaton’s spatial folds had left an afterimage where it had touched the room. The residues lasted several minutes: harmless, silent gestures that made old work continue after the worker had gone.

Guiding a latch through one of Keaton’s folds made Sana look along both paths at once. The case files mentioned prismatic auras after heavy use.

The ghost hand faded at the wrist.

Above them, Sana said, “Left edge is sparking.”

A stool scraped hard. “Give me the gloves.”

“No.”

“I’ll take the reach.”

“You can’t see my latch trace.”

“I can see your pupil.”

“Then look from over there. Stop taking things out of my hands.”

The workshop went still except for the timer. Aveline waited for Keaton to push. She knew the shape of that next minute: concern promoted to authority, refusal treated as ingratitude, every old injury summoned to vote.

Instead, a lamp clicked off.

Keaton said, “Can you still hold the mark?”

“With the visor.”

Cloth whispered across the bench. “It’s beside your right hand.”

“I know where my right hand is.”

“Good news for both of us.” His footsteps retreated. “I’ll move the physical rail. You call the cut.”

“That loses the elegant version.”

“The elegant version whines.”

“That is still not what load means.”

The timer kept ticking. A drawer opened. Sana resumed work, slower now, calling measurements. Keaton rolled the physical rail instead of coming back for her gloves.

Aveline studied the last pale fingers on the wall. “Performance.”

“For us?” Harlan asked.

“They know we’re conscious.”

“Sana is eating. No one commits to sandwich acting that thoroughly.”

“Right-hand collar,” Aveline said. “Old release. I hold the load. You take the locking pin out of phase on three.”

His shoulder tightened. “We haven’t found all the nodes.”

“We don’t need all of them.”

“Your last field just came back late.”

“Because you changed the load.”

“Of course.” His voice had gone light, almost cheerful. That was how he sounded when he wanted a door left unopened. “Pin on three.”

Aveline gathered the collar’s torque into a narrow line. “One.”

Harlan’s weight left her right shoulder.

“Two.”

The pin blurred inside its housing. It did not disappear cleanly. Harlan snapped solid before she reached three, and the collar slammed against the half-phased pin.

The shared spindle spun. Aveline caught the first wrench of force, but the line slipped from her control. The wall boomed. Five seconds later her delayed recoil struck the same anchor and flung their bound hands sideways.

Harlan made a short, animal sound.

“You came back early.”

“Excellent observation.”

His left hand had fallen across her thigh. Aveline closed her fingers around it. He did not close back.

“Squeeze.”

“Doing my best.”

She pressed her thumbnail into his palm.

“Ow,” he said too quickly.

“Where?”

“Palm.”

She had touched the base of his little finger. “Wrong.”

“Close enough for government work.”

“How much can you feel?”

“The frame. Your mood. A powerful sense of regret.”

She pinched harder. Nothing. Her grip tightened until her own wrist band bit.

“How long has your left side been going numb?”

“This is an inconvenient venue.”

“Tuesday, in the barrier collapse—could you feel it then?”

“We need to get out.”

“Friday on the passenger deck?”

“Aveline.”

“Yes or no?”

“Do you want the useful answer, or do you want me guilty before the buyer arrives?”

Locks clacked before she could choose. The cell door opened inward, revealing Sana in a black work suit with her mask pushed onto her head. A prismatic crescent trembled at the left edge of one eye. She carried two foil water pouches and stopped outside the reach of their feet.

“If you keep feeding the spindle, the chest band will crack a rib,” Sana said.

“Release it,” Aveline said.

“No.”

“Return the key.”

“Also no.” Sana fitted a straw to the first pouch and held it where Aveline could drink. “Those are the two large noes. You may have water.”

Aveline drank because refusing would help no one. Sana moved the straw to Harlan, watching his left hand lie open.

“Phase sickness?” she asked.

“Seasonal,” Harlan said.

“Then you picked a bad season.”

She did not offer advice. She checked the color above each wrist band, loosened nothing, and left the water beyond their reach when she went out. The door locked again.

In the workshop, metal struck metal.

Sana said, “The throat is six millimeters wide.”

“Five point eight.”

“It will slip in transport.”

“It won’t crack the jacket.”

“Maybe if you’d measured the case instead of admiring your own geometry—” The sentence cut off. A tool settled onto cloth. “No. You measured it. Give me the blue shims.”

Keaton did not make her ask twice. A tray slid. “Still five point eight.”

“Still ugly. Brace both sides.”

“That was the plan.”

“Then stop looking smug where I can only see half of you.”

The next sounds were two sets of hands working the same brace.

Harlan’s numb fingers twitched against Aveline’s leg.

“Did they just have a better fight than us?” he asked.

“They are transferring stolen rescue equipment to a buyer.”

“That was not my question.”

The phase-key pulsed three times. A receiver answered from the workshop.

Keaton said, “Buyer crossed the outer marker. Thirty-seven minutes.”

Aveline looked at the black pin in her right-hand collar. “I need your usable phase.”

“Had twelve seconds before the dock.”

Not an answer to the question she had asked. A number he could hide inside. “Had?”

“Six on the dock, counting the part where Parallax made the wall arrive sideways. Two just now. Four left if luck has developed professional ethics.”

“And afterward?”

“Left hand first. Jaw if I push. Leg if I’m an idiot.”

“For six weeks?”

“Don’t spend our thirty-seven minutes indicting me.”

“You went on patrol unable to feel half your body.”

“Minutes, not half. And yes.”

She wanted motive, apology, an admission proportionate to the fear opening beneath her ribs. What he had given her were totals. Totals were what he could manage without begging her not to turn him into a patient.

Harlan shifted his chin toward her right wrist. “Your field didn’t slip. You dropped it, and it hit five seconds later.”

“Approximately five.”

“At the dock too.”

The words were flat. No joke to blunt them.

“Yes.”

“You knew.”

“For three weeks.”

His back moved once against hers, a breath stopped and restarted. “So that floor really did throw itself at me.”

“Harlan—”

“No. We’ve established we can both lie in work clothes. Can facts open the door?”

She nearly told him that omission was not the same as lying. The distinction was structurally defensible and useless.

“The pin carries the collar’s stored torque,” she said. “If you remove it while I hold exactly that load, the node shouldn’t see a change. My recoil lands four to six seconds after I release. I can’t narrow it more than that.”

“Four seconds left. Probably three clean.”

“Can you phase only the pin?”

“If you quit moving the target.”

Aveline closed her eyes. The barb was deserved; that did not make it a plan. “I’ll keep the collar fixed. Tell me before sensation moves.”

“And if I say out?”

Her first answer rose ready-made: they were too close to stop once the pin cleared. She swallowed it.

“Then I dump the load into the frame and take whatever comes back.”

“That could tighten us again.”

“Yes.”

It was not reassurance. Harlan’s right shoulder eased anyway.

They began with loads smaller than a held breath. Aveline lifted the torque from one notch of the collar. Harlan brushed the pin with a phased fingertip for less than a second. The nearest node dimmed; a second node answered behind them. Five heartbeats after Aveline released, the frame kicked. This time she had left the line pointed into the ceramic seam, and a hairline crack appeared.

Above, the kitchen timer rang. The extraction rig drew power; both visible nodes faded at once.

“That’s our window,” she said.

“Three clean.”

Harlan took the pin out of phase. Aveline held its torque, rotated the freed collar a finger’s width, and felt the node searching for the missing load.

“Left jaw,” he said. Then, sharper: “Out.”

The collar was almost past the pin. Almost had killed people before.

Aveline let everything go.

The pin resolved in its slot. The spindle took back the fraction she had won. Her recoil jarred the frame five seconds later without widening the crack. Harlan sagged, breathing through his mouth.

Neither spoke until he said, “Jaw’s back.”

“Hand?”

“Two fingers.”

“We wait for all of it.”

“Buyer is at thirty-one.”

Aveline rested her head against his. “Report when the hand is back.”

He was quiet for several ticks. “You stopped.”

“Report, Harlan.”

“Three fingers.”

They waited. The Dacres rolled the physical rail into place overhead. Sana called angles; Keaton repeated only the ones he could not see. When her left vision flashed brighter, she said so. He set the visor closer without touching her gloves. A minute later Aveline heard Sana pick it up.

At the next timer ring, Harlan gave her two clean seconds. He phased the pin. Aveline took the torque, turned the collar clear, and held until the pin returned in empty air.

“Solid,” he said.

She released the stored force with its anchor set in the cracked seam and counted the empty seconds aloud. On five, ceramic split. The node went dark. The right wrist band sprang open, then the chest strap and the remaining bands slackened as the shared spindle unwound.

They rolled apart. Harlan rose with his left arm tucked close and his weight favoring that side. Aveline’s ribs objected when she stood.

“One ugly second,” he said.

“My next recoil is unknown.”

“Our finest hour.”

The broken node had released the cell door. Aveline pushed it open.

The workshop beyond was long and crowded: cell behind them, central bench six paces ahead, extraction cradle bolted above an open copper-mesh case, rear hatch between stacked crates. The phase-key hung in the cradle like a bright splinter. Keaton’s old projections lingered everywhere—one pale shoulder crossing the bench, a hand lifting beside an empty drawer, the outline of Sana leaning briefly into a kiss that had ended long before the real Sana looked up.

“They’re loose,” she said.

Keaton swept both hands apart. Six paces stretched into fifteen. A rolling cabinet seemed to leap into Aveline’s route as the space around it folded.

Sana snapped three latches onto the bench. Black wires sprang between them and caught Harlan across the waist. He went translucent just long enough to pass through, then came solid on the wrong side of the fold, beside the buyer case rather than the key.

“Foot’s gone,” he called. “One second.”

Aveline caught the moving cabinet’s load in her field and fixed it to the floor. “Cabinet held. When I release, four to six.”

Keaton bent the cradle farther away. His stance widened as the fold took strain. Sana worked the key’s jacket with her right hand while her left missed a latch, corrected, and missed again.

“Your mark is splitting,” Keaton said.

“Hold your side.”

“I am holding the room.”

“Then hold it somewhere useful.”

Sana cast a new wire. Aveline caught it before it closed around Harlan and anchored its tension to the cradle brace.

“Retaining pin,” Aveline said. “Can you touch it?”

Harlan looked at the distance Keaton had stretched between them. “One ugly.”

“I can’t give you a count.”

“Then don’t.” He lowered himself onto his good leg. “Tell me when it starts.”

Aveline poured the cabinet’s arrested momentum into the wire and released it. Nothing happened. The return was loose inside its four-to-six-second gap.

Sana heard. She turned the cradle, hiding the pin behind its copper jaw, and hauled on her wire. Aveline let her. The line loaded until it trembled.

The recoil arrived as a wrench through Aveline’s shoulders.

“Now.”

Harlan dropped through the folded distance. For one second his hand and the copper housing occupied the same bright blur. The retaining pin ceased to hold.

Aveline’s returning force ripped along Sana’s wire and through the unpinned brace. The cradle jaw flew open. Harlan struck the buyer case with his solid right hand, knocking its lid away before the phase-key dropped.

Keaton tried to fold the falling key back toward Sana. The projection bowed under the load already in the room; his right arm shook, and one knee hit the floor.

Sana had a latch aimed at the key. She could have fixed it in midair. Instead she struck loose the two latches anchoring Keaton’s far edge.

Space slammed flat. The key fell short of the case.

Aveline caught it in a sling of force and pulled it through the open cell door. The surviving damping nodes seized the motion, winding the key gently against the floor instead of letting it strike.

“Rear hatch,” Keaton said, still on one knee.

Sana tore the buyer’s data wafer from the case and caught the back of his suit. “Move.”

He shortened the distance to the hatch. Sana kept hold of him and the stolen data as they crossed it. Then the steel door shut, leaving their pale afterimages to finish gestures the Dacres no longer had time for.

Harlan sat down where he had landed. Aveline managed two steps before the spent field folded her beside him. She turned until their backs met again. This time the position kept pressure off her ribs and let them watch both doors.

The phase-key hummed safely in the broken cell. The buyer signal blinked in its empty case.

Harlan reached the confiscated gear tray with his right hand and found his phone. “Dispatch or clinic?”

“Dispatch.”

He unlocked the screen. “Clinic after.”

“Before debrief.”

“There goes tomorrow’s patrol.”

“Delete it.”

He dialed. While it rang, Aveline said, “Nine o’clock. Kitchen table. Not the gear room.”

“Clinic at nine.”

“Then noon.”

His thumb hovered over the speaker button. “No case files?”

“Leave them at the office.”

The dispatcher answered. Harlan asked for recovery and medical support, gave the workshop coordinates, then described the numbness without rounding down. When he called Aveline’s recoil a timing problem, she leaned toward the phone.

“Uncontrolled,” she said. “Four to six seconds. For three weeks.”

“Put that in too,” he told the dispatcher.
